newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong executives paid too much - study.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong executives paid too much - study.

text.p: The pay cheques of Hong Kong's top executives could be too fat and were not linked to corporate performance, the South China Morning Post said on Monday.
A study, carried out by the City University of Hong Kong, found it was not uncommon for executives in Hong Kong to get paid on a par with some of the largest firms in the United States.
"In some extreme cases, total executive pay may even exceed the current year net profits of the entire firm," researchers Bob Chan, Joey Chan and Stephen Leung said.
The study looked at the remuneration packages of more than 1,500 companies between 1990 and 1994, the paper said.
They found the reason for the big pay cheques was because Hong Kong's top executives owned more of the listed company concerned than their U.S. counterparts, it said.
As for directors, the researchers found it was not uncommon that they were paid more than the actual profit at the group, it said.
"There is a total of 132 cases in our sample. In one extreme case, total director compensations were 76 times the net profits," the researchers said.
They also found that "firm (company) performance does not have influence on director compensation", it said.
